title: Designing classes and interfaces
idea: Good class design gives each class one job and hidden state, and lets classes talk only through small interfaces of the methods callers need.
points: Nouns in the requirements suggest classes; verbs suggest their methods.
Give each class one reason to change and keep its state private.
An interface is the set of methods a caller relies on.
In JavaScript, write one as a base class whose methods throw.

hero.title: One big class versus focused ones

left.title: One `OrderManager` does all
items: Validates, prices, charges cards and sends emails
Creates its own payment client inside
Tests need a real payment provider

right.title: Focused classes, narrow interfaces
items: `Checkout` coordinates; each job has its own class
A new provider is one new class
Tests pass a fake gateway in

hero.verdict: Split classes by job, and connect them through the smallest interface that works.

code.title: Program to an interface
code.caption: `Checkout` knows only `charge()`. Write a `DeclineAllGateway` and pass it in instead.

walk.text: The interface: a base class whose method throws until a subclass overrides it.
One implementation. A real provider would be another subclass.
`Checkout` receives its gateway and keeps it private.
It calls only the interface method, never provider details.

code.title: Guard the invariants
code.caption: A value class that rejects bad input in its constructor and never changes after creation. `add` returns a new `Money`.

pitfalls: Expose behaviour such as `add()`, not a getter and setter for every field.
Keep interfaces small; callers should not depend on methods they never use.
Validate in the constructor so no object exists in a broken state.

options: TypeError: save is not a function
quiz.why: `MemStore` named its method `put`, so `save` is found on `Store` and throws. The base class caught the missing override.

takeaway: One job per class; talk through small interfaces.
